question: what is their explanation for the effectiveness of back-translation?

extractive_spans: when using BT, cases where the source is shorter than the target are rarer; cases when they have the same length are more frequent
automatic word alignments between artificial sources tend to be more monotonic than when using natural sources
evidence: Comparing the natural and artificial sources of our parallel data wrt. several linguistic and distributional properties, we observe that (see Fig. FIGREF21 - FIGREF22 ):
artificial sources are on average shorter than natural ones: when using BT, cases where the source is shorter than the target are rarer; cases when they have the same length are more frequent.

automatic word alignments between artificial sources tend to be more monotonic than when using natural sources, as measured by the average Kendall INLINEFORM0 of source-target alignments BIBREF22 : for French-English the respective numbers are 0.048 (natural) and 0.018 (artificial); for German-English 0.068 and 0.053. Using more monotonic sentence pairs turns out to be a facilitating factor for NMT, as also noted by BIBREF20 .

The intuition is that properties (i) and (ii) should help translation as compared to natural source, while property (iv) should be detrimental. We checked (ii) by building systems with only 10M words from the natural parallel data selecting these data either randomly or based on the regularity of their word alignments. Results in Table TABREF23 show that the latter is much preferable for the overall performance. This might explain that the mostly monotonic BT from Moses are almost as good as the fluid BT from NMT and that both boost the baseline.

title: Using Monolingual Data in Neural Machine Translation: a Systematic Study
answer_short: BT is effective because artificial sources are more monotonic and syntactically simpler, which facilitates NMT, even though they are lexically less diverse and can encourage overfitting.
answer_rationale: The explanation for the effectiveness of back-translation (BT) is rooted in the properties of artificial data generated through BT. According to the retrieved documents, BT produces artificial sources that are more monotonic (as measured by Kendall’s tau) and syntactically simpler than natural sources, which facilitates NMT performance. For example, Text 3 and Text 6 highlight that monotonicity and syntactic simplicity are beneficial factors. However, BT also encourages overfitting, as shown in Text 2, which notes that BT data does not act as a regularizer and may even hinder generalization. Despite this, the overall effectiveness of BT is confirmed in Text 5, which states that BT is very effective and provides new explanations for its success, including the properties of the generated data.
